title: Harvey Power Users: The New Generation of Legal Change Agent
author: Reena SenGupta

dom.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s view that value depends on organisational adoption rather than tool acquisition alone, and materially extends it by identifying power users as an internal change-management mechanism. Its customer-study figures also provide selected evidence of substantial time savings, while its claimed competitive advantage remains predictive and company-sponsored rather than proof of durable infrastructure or wider business-model disruption.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI’s value depends on user fluency and workflow redesign, then materially extends the cluster by identifying power users as internal change agents who can spread effective practices. Its reported time savings support task-level productivity gains, while the absence of formal ROI frameworks and quantified cost savings reinforces the distinction between user-level gains and realised organisational value.

kp.k: Customer research identifies substantial power-user time savings
kp.d: Writing on January 29, 2026, SenGupta reports findings from RSGI's study with Harvey conducted the previous year across 40 customers. Typically, 20-30% of lawyers at the 29 participating law firms were classified by their firms as power users, defined through volume or strategic use. These users saved nearly 37 hours monthly, double standard users; in-house power users saved 28.3 hours versus 11.8 for standard users. These are reported customer-study findings, rather than evidence of quantified financial savings.
qs: RSGI did with Harvey last year on its usage with 40 customers.
Typically, 20-30% of the lawyers at the 29 participating law firms in the report could be categorised as power users.
(Law firms defined the power users themselves as being either volume or strategic users.)
These power users saved nearly 37 hours per month, double the amount compared to standard users. For in-house legal teams, power users save 28.3 hours per month compared to 11.8 for standard users.

kp.k: Power users span seniority levels, including equity partners
kp.d: The author reports that adoption was not confined to younger lawyers and that older partners were as likely to be keen Harvey adopters. Customer quotations carried in the blog illustrate this: Schoenherr reports heavy use even among equity partners, while Jackson Walker attributes partners' process-improvement contributions to their knowledge of existing pain points.
qs: Older partners were as likely to be a keen adopter of Harvey.
We see power users on all levels. Even equity partners are heavy users. It is super exciting.
Partners are the most vocal and are finding the best ways to streamline processes with Harvey. They know where the pain points are and what can be done better.

kp.k: Workflow redesign distinguishes power users from simple augmentation
kp.d: SenGupta proposes a fluency mechanism in which prompting expertise, workflow design and collaboration compound AI's impact. She asserts that power users are more likely to change how work is done than merely augment existing work, describing exponentially increasing fluency and benefits and claiming they are more than twice as productive and effective. The article presents these as broader authorial claims without specifying a separate effectiveness measure.
qs: as teams develop expertise in prompting, workflow design, and collaboration, impact compounds.
One of the characteristics of a power user is that they are more likely to change how they do work, rather than just use Harvey as an augmentation tool.
Their fluency rises exponentially, as do the benefits they see from using Harvey or other AI.
They are more than twice as productive and as effective, often able to create a flywheel effect in their practices.

kp.k: Peer influence supports change, but heavy use differs
kp.d: The article reports firms deploying power users as innovation champions and cultural change agents, while preserving participating firms' qualification that some are simply heavy users. As cross-domain support for peer-led learning, it cites learning-platform company Degreed's finding that 55% of employees generally seek colleagues' advice when learning new skills, using this to argue that internal power users can be more influential than external trainers.
qs: They are becoming rapid enablers of cultural change within the firms.

Degreed, a US-based, learning experience platform found that 55% of employees generally turn to colleagues for advice when learning new skills, making internal power users more influential than external trainers.
Some of the firms in the Harvey report did point out that not all power users are change agents. Some are just heavy users.

kp.k: Immediate productivity gains lack quantified financial returns
kp.d: SenGupta contrasts some practice-area experiences with Erik Brynjolfsson's reported j-curve account, under which transformative technology initially depresses productivity while companies invest in restructuring. She reports immediate productivity gains across the studied firms, but qualifies that most had not implemented formal institutional Harvey ROI frameworks and had not yet quantified cost savings.
qs: Here, he points out that there is often a dip in productivity following the adoption of a transformative technology, where companies invest time and capital into restructuring before seeing the benefits.

While law firms in the report had not, in the main, implemented formal and institutional ‘ROI’ (return-on-investment) frameworks for Harvey, they were seeing immediate productivity gains across the board albeit not quantifiable cost savings — yet.

kp.k: AI expertise may reshape authority for organisational change
kp.d: The author argues that firms have historically selected popular, influential lawyers for leadership and mistakenly expected people pleasers to deliver change. Drawing on change consultant John Amaechi's distinction between charisma and competence, she suggests AI power users could instead lead through demonstrated workflow redesign and helping colleagues work differently. This is an argument about potential change leadership, not a documented shift in formal governance.
qs: For the first time, the lawyers tasked with change may not be the people pleaser or those with the most social charisma and fee-earning clout. They may be the AI power user.
John Amaechi OBE, the change consultant points out that it is important not to mistake charisma for competence.
These digitally enabled partners and lawyers - who can lead by example, restructure workflows and show colleagues how to work better and smarter - have a moment in the sun.

kp.k: Workplace fulfilment is linked to renewed professional engagement
kp.d: The article reports that 83% of Harvey study participants agreed or strongly agreed that Harvey positively affected workplace fulfilment. SenGupta interprets this as relief from drudgery and renewed enthusiasm for practising law, linking engaged power users to the possibility of more effective change agents. The percentage concerns study participants, not explicitly only power users.
qs: One of the impacts of Harvey is that it has removed the drudgery from legal work: 83% of the Harvey study participants agreed or strongly agreed that its impact on workplace fulfilment was positive.
They have fallen in love with being lawyers again.
These happy power users can be a cohort of change agents unlike any that law firms have seen before.

kp.k: Coordinating power users could confer competitive advantage
kp.d: SenGupta predicts that firms organising and coordinating their power users are likely to gain an advantage, while acknowledging that these lawyers remain constrained by existing firm systems and hierarchies. This is a conditional strategic recommendation rather than a measured competitive outcome.
qs: They still have challenges and must work within existing law firm systems and hierarchies but the firm that organises and co-ordinates their power users is likely to get ahead of the game.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: SenGupta claims that AI power users achieve greater time savings, redesign legal workflows, and can become influential agents of organisational change.
pts.d: SenGupta reports that law-firm power users save nearly 37 hours per month, roughly twice standard users' savings, while in-house power users save 28.3 hours compared with 11.8 for standard users. She proposes a 'Harvey Fluency Curve': expertise in prompting, workflow design and collaboration compounds benefits. She further claims that power users are more than twice as productive and effective, and are more likely to change how work is done rather than simply augment existing work. These broader productivity and effectiveness claims are distinct from the reported time-saving figures. She describes immediate productivity gains, though not yet quantifiable cost savings, and argues that AI reduces drudgery and improves workplace fulfilment. Her organisational prediction is that firms coordinating power users as change agents are likely to gain an advantage, potentially shifting change leadership away from lawyers selected principally for popularity, charisma or fee-earning influence.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source draws on an RSGI–Harvey customer report, participating firms' accounts, a general workplace-learning statistic, and change-management commentary.
pts.d: In this Harvey company-blog article, SenGupta cites RSGI's report with Harvey on usage among 40 customers, including 29 participating law firms. Firms classified power users themselves as volume or strategic users; typically 20–30% of lawyers at participating firms fell into that category. The report supplies the monthly time-saving comparisons and a finding that 83% of study participants agreed or strongly agreed that workplace fulfilment improved. Accounts attributed to Schoenherr and Jackson Walker support the claim that adoption and process improvement extend to partners. SenGupta cites Degreed's finding that 55% of employees generally turn to colleagues when learning skills to support her argument about internal influence; this is general workplace evidence, not a legal-sector-specific result. She invokes John Amaechi's distinction between charisma and competence as a change-management framing and contrasts reported immediate gains with Erik Brynjolfsson's productivity j-curve. The article does not present a separate measurement basis for exponential fluency gains or the assertion that power users are more than twice as effective. It explicitly notes that most reporting firms lacked formal institutional ROI frameworks.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article presents current adoption benefits as of January 2026, drawing on a report from the previous year, and makes conditional predictions without a fixed future deadline.
pts.d: Published on January 29, 2026, the article refers to the RSGI–Harvey report as having been conducted 'last year', implying 2025. SenGupta locates accelerated professional change in the preceding five years, particularly the last 18 months, attributing changing working patterns to Covid and generative AI. Time savings are expressed per month. Compounding benefits depend on developing expertise in prompting, workflow design and collaboration. Immediate productivity gains are reported for firms in the study, but quantifiable cost savings had not yet been established. The change-agent argument is qualified: some power users are merely heavy users, and even effective champions operate within existing hierarchies. The predicted competitive advantage depends on firms organising and coordinating these users; no deadline or quantified future advantage is specified.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims primarily concern lawyers and leadership within adopting law firms, with separate time-saving evidence for in-house legal teams.
pts.d: Law-firm lawyers across seniority levels, including older and equity partners, are described as potential power users rather than adoption being confined to younger lawyers. Power users themselves reportedly gain time, effectiveness and fulfilment; colleagues may benefit from peer learning and redesigned workflows. Practice groups and firms may experience cultural change and competitive benefits when leadership coordinates these users. Schoenherr's account concerns adoption at all levels, while Jackson Walker's account identifies partners as vocal process-improvement leaders. In-house teams are a separate affected group with their own reported monthly savings. The article does not specify consequences for legal employment levels, fees, client outcomes, ALSPs or access to justice.
